title: Book 02 — Chapter 4: Revised Exam Questions and Model Answers

source.title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
source.author: Ayatullah Murtadha Mutahhari
source.method: Questions were checked against the original Al-Islam.org chapter. Political motives are attributed as interpretations where the source treats them as hypotheses; the Imam’s rejection of the Mahdi claim is distinguished from his willingness to support resistance to oppression.

revision_policy: Exam-ready model answers with historical sequence and reasoning made explicit.
Do not confuse Abu Salmah’s political offer with a sincere, organized transfer of authority.
Distinguish Imam al-Sadiq’s rejection of a false Mahdi identification from his willingness to support a just uprising.
Limit claims about the intellectual movements of the period to what the chapter actually states.

questions.unit_title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
questions.prompt: What political opportunity arose during the lifetime of Imam al-Sadiq, and why did Mutahhari consider it significant?
questions.answer: The end of Umayyad rule and the beginning of Abbasid rule created a major political opening. Opposition to the Umayyads had grown among Arabs and Persians because of their religious misconduct, despotic rule, and persecution of pious Muslims and descendants of the Prophet. Alawi uprisings, especially those of Zayd ibn ‘Ali and his son Yahya, had also weakened the Umayyads’ reputation and prepared the ground for revolt. Mutahhari asks why Imam al-Sadiq did not take advantage of this opportunity to seize political leadership. The chapter explains that the Abbasids had organized the movement and that the apparent opening did not provide the Imam with a genuine or trustworthy path to authority.
questions.source_locator: Opening question — Why did Imam al-Sadiq decline a major political opening?

questions.unit_title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
questions.prompt: What religious and worldly factors contributed to the growing opposition against the Umayyads?
questions.answer: Mutahhari identifies both religious and worldly causes. Religiously, the Umayyads had committed repeated acts of debauchery, tyranny, and crimes against eminent and pious Muslims. Their conduct, especially after the martyrdom of Imam al-Husayn, damaged their religious reputation. Politically and socially, their rule was oppressive, with officials such as Hajjaj ibn Yusuf exercising extreme cruelty. These conditions produced widespread discontent among Arabs and Persians, particularly in Khorasan. Mutahhari emphasizes that the opposition was not simply an ethnic or Iranian nationalist movement; it was also driven by religious anger against a ruling system seen as violating Islamic principles.
questions.source_locator: Opening question — Why did Imam al-Sadiq decline a major political opening?

questions.unit_title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
questions.prompt: How did the uprisings of Zayd ibn ‘Ali and Yahya ibn Zayd affect the political atmosphere, especially in Khorasan?
questions.answer: Zayd ibn ‘Ali’s uprising and the later revolt of his son Yahya had a lasting influence even though both were defeated. Zayd was killed near Kufa and his body was publicly displayed for a long period. Yahya later went to Khorasan, where he gained extraordinary popularity before being killed by the Umayyads. Mutahhari reports that when the people of Khorasan later rose against the Umayyads, they mourned Yahya for seventy days. He uses this to show that failed uprisings could still prepare the emotional and political ground for later movements. By the end of the Umayyad period, widespread discontent existed, although it had not yet become a fully organized revolution.
questions.source_locator: Opening question — Why did Imam al-Sadiq decline a major political opening?

questions.unit_title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
questions.prompt: Who were the three Abbasid brothers who organized the movement against the Umayyads?
questions.answer: Mutahhari identifies the three brothers as Ibrahim al-Imam, Abu al-‘Abbas al-Saffah, and Abu Ja‘far al-Mansur. They belonged to the line of ‘Abbas ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet’s uncle. They used the widespread dissatisfaction with Umayyad rule to organize a secret movement, appointing preachers and representatives in different regions while keeping their own identities and political objectives concealed. The chapter emphasizes that the Abbasid rise was not a spontaneous popular movement; it was carefully organized by a family that intended to gain control of the caliphate.
questions.source_locator: The Abbasids’ utilization of the people’s discontentment

questions.unit_title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
questions.prompt: What slogan did the Abbasid movement use, and what did it communicate to the people?
questions.answer: The Abbasids used the slogan al-Rida or al-Radi, meaning a chosen or approved person from the Household of the Prophet. They did not initially name a specific candidate, which allowed the movement to attract people who hoped for leadership from the Ahl al-Bayt without revealing the Abbasids’ own plans. Mutahhari argues that the movement’s public language was Islamic and centred on the Prophet’s Household, not on Iranian nationalism. The slogan enabled the Abbasids to benefit from the religious feelings and political hopes of people who opposed Umayyad oppression.
questions.source_locator: The Abbasids’ utilization of the people’s discontentment

questions.unit_title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
questions.prompt: Why does Mutahhari reject the claim that the Abbasid uprising was primarily an Iranian nationalist movement?
questions.answer: Mutahhari points to the movement’s slogans and public appeals. The Abbasids called people to rise in the name of Islam and the Household of the Prophet, not in the name of Iranian ethnicity. Their banners used Qur’anic verses about defending the oppressed and about human equality before God, directly challenging Umayyad Arab preference and discrimination. Mutahhari argues that the people of Khorasan could have chosen ethnic or national slogans, but they deliberately used Islamic ones. He therefore rejects the claim that the uprising was simply driven by Iranian nationalism and interprets it as a movement that appealed to religious opposition to Umayyad rule.
questions.source_locator: The Abbasids’ utilization of the people’s discontentment

questions.unit_title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
questions.prompt: What roles did Abu Muslim and Abu Salmah Khallal play in the Abbasid movement?
questions.answer: Abu Muslim was sent by the Abbasids to Khorasan, where he became the movement’s leading military commander. Mutahhari says that he did not originate the uprising; the Abbasids had already sent missionaries and organized the network. Abu Salmah Khallal led the movement in Kufa and was regarded as a highly capable politician and speaker. The Abbasids gave Abu Salmah the title “Minister of the Family of Muhammad” and Abu Muslim the title “Prince of the Family of Muhammad.” Abu Salmah was described as politically superior to Abu Muslim, which contributed to rivalry between them.
questions.source_locator: The Abbasids’ utilization of the people’s discontentment — Abu Muslim and Abu Salmah

questions.unit_title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
questions.prompt: Why did Abu Muslim arrange the killing of Abu Salmah?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says Abu Muslim was jealous of Abu Salmah and viewed him as a rival. He repeatedly wrote to al-Saffah and other Abbasid relatives, accusing Abu Salmah of being dangerous and suggesting that he wanted to return the caliphate to the family of Abu Talib. Al-Saffah was initially reluctant to kill a man who had served him faithfully and did not consider the accusation proven. Abu Muslim eventually arranged Abu Salmah’s murder himself, using a group that included people connected with the caliph’s household. The episode reveals the rivalry and violence within the Abbasid movement even before its power had fully consolidated.
questions.source_locator: The Abbasids’ utilization of the people’s discontentment — Abu Muslim and Abu Salmah

questions.unit_title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
questions.prompt: To whom did Abu Salmah send his confidential letters, and what did he offer them?
questions.answer: According to the account Mutahhari discusses from Mas‘udi, Abu Salmah sent two copies of the same confidential letter to Imam Ja‘far al-Sadiq and ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd. He instructed the courier to deliver each letter privately and not tell either recipient that the same offer had been made to the other. In the letter, Abu Salmah claimed that the caliphate was effectively in his hands and that he could change the political situation in favour of the recipient if they agreed. The arrangement shows that he was seeking a candidate from the Prophet’s family who could provide legitimacy to a political transfer of power.
questions.source_locator: Abu Salmah’s letter to Imam al-Sadiq and ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd

questions.unit_title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
questions.prompt: How did Imam al-Sadiq respond when Abu Salmah’s letter was delivered to him?
questions.answer: When the courier described Abu Salmah as one of the Imam’s followers, Imam al-Sadiq immediately replied that Abu Salmah was not his follower. He then asked for fire, burned the letter without reading it, and instructed the courier to deliver a poem as his response. The poem compared Abu Salmah to a person who gathers firewood and places it on someone else’s rope, allowing another person to collect the benefit of his labour. Mutahhari explains that the Imam was warning Abu Salmah that he had worked to establish Abbasid power, only for another person to take the results. The Imam refused to become a tool in Abu Salmah’s political manoeuvre.
questions.source_locator: The reaction of Imam al-Sadiq and ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd — Burning the letter

questions.unit_title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
questions.prompt: What did Imam al-Sadiq ask ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd when he presented Abu Salmah’s letter, and why?
questions.answer: When ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd excitedly told the Imam that the people of Khorasan were ready to return the caliphate to his family, the Imam asked whether the people of Khorasan were really his followers. He asked whether ‘Abd Allah had sent Abu Muslim to Khorasan, instructed the people to wear black, or personally brought the Khorasani supporters to Medina. The questions exposed the weakness of the claim: the movement had been organized by the Abbasids, not by ‘Abd Allah or his followers. Mutahhari uses this exchange to show that the Imam distinguished popular religious slogans from actual political control and organization.
questions.source_locator: The reaction of Imam al-Sadiq and ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd — Testing the claim of popular support

questions.unit_title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
questions.prompt: How does Mutahhari interpret Abu Salmah’s decision to send the same letter to both Imam al-Sadiq and ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd?
questions.answer: Mutahhari interprets the double letter as a political manoeuvre rather than a sincere religious offer. Abu Salmah wanted to find a prominent member of the Prophet’s family whom the public would accept, but he did not want to commit himself to one candidate. By sending identical offers to Imam al-Sadiq and ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd without telling either about the other, he kept both possibilities open and intended to use whichever candidate accepted. Mutahhari describes this as an attempt to place a political figure in power as a tool, not as a carefully prepared and sincere transfer of legitimate authority.
questions.source_locator: The reaction of Imam al-Sadiq and ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd — Testing the claim of popular support

questions.unit_title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
questions.prompt: Why does Mutahhari say there were no real conditions for Imam al-Sadiq to accept Abu Salmah’s offer?
questions.answer: Mutahhari argues that neither the spiritual nor the practical conditions for a legitimate transfer of power existed. There was no evidence that the offer came from people with pure intentions who genuinely recognized the Imam’s leadership. Nor were there visible resources, organized support, or a trustworthy political structure that could sustain a transfer of authority. Abu Salmah was a political operator who had helped the Abbasids gain power and was now seeking a candidate to serve his own strategy. Imam al-Sadiq therefore had no reason to risk becoming an instrument in a plan that lacked both moral legitimacy and practical foundations.
questions.source_locator: The reaction of Imam al-Sadiq and ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd — Testing the claim of popular support

questions.unit_title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
questions.prompt: Where and when did the secret gathering of the heads of Bani Hashim take place, and what was proposed there?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that the heads of Bani Hashim met secretly at Abwa’, a place between Mecca and Medina, near twelve years before the Abbasid uprising in Khorasan. Those present included ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd, his sons Muhammad and Ibrahim, the Abbasid brothers, and members of their wider family. ‘Abd Allah proposed that they pledge allegiance to his young son Muhammad and make him the leader of the movement against the Umayyads. The meeting is important because it shows that the proposal to identify Muhammad as a future leader existed long before Abu Salmah’s later letter.
questions.source_locator: The secret gathering of the heads of Bani Hashim

questions.unit_title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
questions.prompt: Why did some people identify Muhammad Nafs Zakiyyah as the Promised Mahdi?
questions.answer: Muhammad Nafs Zakiyyah was the son of ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd. His name was Muhammad, like the Prophet’s, his father’s name was ‘Abd Allah, and he reportedly had a mark on his shoulder resembling a sign mentioned in traditions about the Mahdi. His lineage was also significant: ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd was descended from Imam al-Hasan through his father and from Imam al-Husayn through his mother. These features led some people, including members of the family, to believe that Muhammad was the promised Mahdi. Mutahhari explains that these identifying similarities were not sufficient to establish that he was the actual Mahdi.
questions.source_locator: Allegiance with Muhammad Nafs al-Zakiyyah — Lineage is not proof of being the Mahdi

questions.unit_title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
questions.prompt: What distinction did Imam al-Sadiq make between supporting Muhammad Nafs Zakiyyah’s uprising and accepting him as the Promised Mahdi?
questions.answer: Imam al-Sadiq refused to pledge allegiance to Muhammad Nafs Zakiyyah under the claim that he was the Promised Mahdi. He said that Muhammad was not the Mahdi foretold by the Prophet and that the time for that promised appearance had not arrived. However, the Imam stated that if the purpose of the uprising was to enjoin good, forbid evil, and oppose oppression, he would be willing to pledge allegiance and support it. The distinction is essential: Imam al-Sadiq did not reject resistance to tyranny; he rejected a false religious identification being used to justify the movement. The moral purpose of the uprising and the truth of the Mahdi claim had to be judged separately.
questions.source_locator: Allegiance with Muhammad Nafs al-Zakiyyah — Supporting justice without accepting an unproven title

questions.unit_title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
questions.prompt: What did Imam al-Sadiq predict about Muhammad Nafs Zakiyyah and the role of Mansur?
questions.answer: Imam al-Sadiq warned ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd that his son Muhammad was not the Promised Mahdi and would be killed rather than become caliph. The Imam also indicated that the Abbasid ruler Mansur would be responsible for killing the sons of ‘Abd Allah. He identified Mansur, who was wearing a yellow cloak at the gathering, and predicted that the same man would later kill them. Mutahhari recounts that the prediction was later confirmed when Mansur killed Muhammad and another son of ‘Abd Allah. The episode demonstrates the Imam’s knowledge of the political danger and his concern for Muhammad, whom he loved despite rejecting the Mahdi claim.
questions.source_locator: Allegiance with Muhammad Nafs al-Zakiyyah — Supporting justice without accepting an unproven title

questions.unit_title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
questions.prompt: Explain how the Abbasids turned widespread opposition to the Umayyads into an organized movement, and why Mutahhari says its slogans were Islamic rather than nationalist.
questions.answer: Mutahhari describes widespread opposition to the Umayyads arising from religious misconduct, political oppression, and the persecution of the Ahl al-Bayt. The uprisings of Zayd ibn ‘Ali and Yahya ibn Zayd further damaged Umayyad legitimacy, especially in Khorasan, where people continued to mourn Yahya long after his death. The Abbasids used this discontent by organizing secret networks, sending missionaries, and establishing centres in Iraq, Hijaz, Syria, and Khorasan. Their slogans referred to al-Rida or al-Radi, a chosen person from the Prophet’s Household, and their public banners carried Qur’anic verses about defending the oppressed and human equality. Mutahhari argues that the movement deliberately appealed to Islamic principles rather than Iranian ethnic identity. Abu Muslim became its leading commander in Khorasan, while Abu Salmah led its organization in Kufa. The movement’s success therefore rested on organized political activity that appropriated genuine religious discontent.
questions.source_locator: The Abbasids’ utilization of the people’s discontentment

questions.unit_title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
questions.prompt: Compare the roles of Abu Muslim and Abu Salmah in the Abbasid movement, including their rivalry and its consequences.
questions.answer: Abu Muslim was sent by the Abbasids to Khorasan and became the movement’s leading military commander. Mutahhari emphasizes that he did not create the uprising; the Abbasids had already organized the network and sent missionaries. Abu Salmah Khallal was the leading figure in Kufa and was considered more politically sophisticated, with strong oratory and diplomatic abilities. The Abbasids called him the “Minister of the Family of Muhammad” and Abu Muslim the “Prince of the Family of Muhammad.” Their rivalry became intense because Abu Muslim was jealous of Abu Salmah’s position. He repeatedly accused Abu Salmah of secretly wanting to transfer the caliphate to the family of Abu Talib. When al-Saffah hesitated to act, Abu Muslim arranged Abu Salmah’s murder himself. The episode reveals the political ambition, suspicion, and violence within the Abbasid movement.
questions.source_locator: The Abbasids’ utilization of the people’s discontentment — Abu Muslim and Abu Salmah

questions.unit_title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
questions.prompt: Analyze Imam al-Sadiq’s burning of Abu Salmah’s letter and the meaning of the poem he sent as his response.
questions.answer: When Abu Salmah’s courier delivered the letter, Imam al-Sadiq rejected the description of Abu Salmah as his follower and burned the letter without reading it. He then sent a poem comparing Abu Salmah to someone who gathers firewood but places it on another person’s rope, allowing that person to collect the reward of his labour. Mutahhari explains that the Imam was warning Abu Salmah that he had worked to establish Abbasid power, but another person would take the benefit. The Imam refused to enter a political arrangement in which he would become a tool for a man whose intentions and resources were not trustworthy. The act of burning the letter was therefore a clear rejection, while the poem explained the political miscalculation behind Abu Salmah’s offer.
questions.source_locator: The reaction of Imam al-Sadiq and ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd — Burning the letter

questions.unit_title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
questions.prompt: Compare the reactions of Imam al-Sadiq and ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd to Abu Salmah’s identical letters. What does the contrast reveal?
questions.answer: Imam al-Sadiq immediately rejected Abu Salmah’s letter, burned it without reading it, and sent a poem warning that Abu Salmah’s political work would benefit someone else. He also denied that Abu Salmah was his follower. ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd, by contrast, became excited and interpreted the letter as proof that the people of Khorasan were ready to return the caliphate to his family. When he approached the Imam, the Imam challenged his claim that the Khorasani people were his followers and reminded him that he had not organized their movement. The contrast reveals the difference between political excitement and careful judgment. The Imam recognized that Abu Salmah was a political operator offering the same proposal to two candidates, while ‘Abd Allah was attracted by the promise of power and accepted the claim too readily.
questions.source_locator: The reaction of Imam al-Sadiq and ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd — Testing the claim of popular support

questions.unit_title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
questions.prompt: Describe the secret gathering at Abwa’ and explain how the proposal to make Muhammad Nafs Zakiyyah a leader developed.
questions.answer: Mutahhari recounts that the heads of Bani Hashim met at Abwa’, a place between Mecca and Medina, nearly twelve years before the Abbasid uprising in Khorasan. The gathering included ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd, his sons Muhammad and Ibrahim, the Abbasid brothers, and other relatives. ‘Abd Allah proposed that they pledge allegiance to his son Muhammad and make him the leader of the anti-Umayyad movement. Muhammad was later identified by some as the Promised Mahdi because he shared the Prophet’s name, had a father named ‘Abd Allah, and reportedly bore a mark on his shoulder resembling a sign in Mahdist traditions. Mutahhari explains that the family’s political hopes and the public expectation of the Mahdi became intertwined, but Imam al-Sadiq rejected the claim that Muhammad was the promised figure.

questions.unit_title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
questions.prompt: Why was Imam al-Sadiq willing to support an uprising against oppression but unwilling to pledge allegiance to Muhammad Nafs Zakiyyah as the Mahdi?
questions.answer: Imam al-Sadiq distinguished the moral purpose of resistance from the truth of the religious claim used to justify it. He stated that Muhammad Nafs Zakiyyah was not the Promised Mahdi and that the time for the Mahdi’s appearance had not arrived. Therefore, he would not pledge allegiance to Muhammad under the title of the Mahdi of the nation. However, he explicitly said that if the people intended to enjoin good, forbid evil, and fight oppression, he was prepared to support the uprising. His refusal was not a rejection of resistance or a desire to preserve Umayyad rule. It was a refusal to attach a false doctrinal claim to a political movement. Mutahhari uses this distinction to show that a just cause must be pursued under truthful principles and cannot be legitimized by an incorrect claim about the Mahdi.
questions.source_locator: Allegiance with Muhammad Nafs al-Zakiyyah — Supporting justice without accepting an unproven title

questions.unit_title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
questions.prompt: How did the events after the Abwa’ gathering confirm Imam al-Sadiq’s warning about Muhammad Nafs Zakiyyah and Mansur?
questions.answer: At the gathering, Imam al-Sadiq warned that Muhammad Nafs Zakiyyah would not become caliph and would instead be killed. He also identified Mansur, who was present wearing a yellow cloak, as the person who would later kill the sons of ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd. A witness, ‘Abd al-‘Aziz ibn ‘Imran al-Zuhri, initially thought the Imam might be speaking out of jealousy because everyone was pledging allegiance to Muhammad. Later, he saw Mansur kill Muhammad and another son of ‘Abd Allah, and recognized that the Imam’s warning had been fulfilled. Mutahhari also notes that Imam al-Sadiq loved Muhammad and wept when he saw him, which counters the accusation that the Imam rejected him out of jealousy. The episode demonstrates the Imam’s concern and the danger hidden behind the political promises made at the gathering.
questions.source_locator: Allegiance with Muhammad Nafs al-Zakiyyah — Supporting justice without accepting an unproven title

questions.unit_title: Chapter 4: Imam al-Sadiq and the Issue of Vicegerency (Sessions 1 & 2)
questions.prompt: Why does Mutahhari argue that Imam al-Sadiq’s historical circumstances called for intellectual leadership rather than a repetition of Imam al-Husayn’s armed uprising?
questions.answer: Mutahhari explains that Imam al-Sadiq lived in a period very different from Imam al-Husayn’s. Imam al-Husayn’s time was marked by severe political suppression, and very few sayings from that period were preserved. By the time of Imam al-Sadiq, the Muslim world had expanded, new communities had entered Islam, books were being translated, and a wide range of intellectual movements had emerged. There were debates about atheism, mysticism, jurisprudence, and other religious and philosophical questions. The political conflicts between the Umayyads and Abbasids also created an opportunity for scholarly activity. Mutahhari notes that the names of approximately four thousand students are associated with Imam al-Sadiq. He argues that if Imam al-Sadiq had been martyred in the same way as Imam al-Husayn, the vast intellectual movement he led would not have taken place. His historical responsibility therefore required a different form of struggle: preserving and expanding Islamic knowledge and guidance.
questions.source_locator: Characteristics of Imam al-Sadiq’s time
